context: Current closing price of Berkshire Hathaway B (BRK-B): $504.78 USD as of 2026-07-02.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, likely around 503–505 for SPY or a similar broad equity index. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the recent close with only a small positive drift, reflecting the historical tendency for equity markets to grind slightly higher on any given day when no major catalyst is present. At one week, I added a bit more drift to account for the multi-day compounding of that positive expected return, while at one month the drift becomes more meaningful in absolute terms even though it remains modest relative to the overall price level. In all three cases, the point estimates essentially encode a mild bullish bias consistent with the long-run equity risk premium, rather than any specific directional thesis.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by realized volatility scaling with the square root of time. Daily SPY volatility tends to run around 0.8–1.2% in normal regimes, so a one-day 90% interval spanning roughly 19 points (about ±1.9%) reflects something close to two standard deviations of daily moves. As the horizon extends to a week, I scaled that uncertainty up accordingly, producing a roughly 38-point wide interval, and by one month the interval widens to about 76 points. These widths also implicitly account for the possibility that volatility itself is not constant — realized vol can spike meaningfully during risk-off episodes, which fattens the tails beyond what a simple Gaussian assumption would suggest.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include a sudden policy shock such as an unexpected Federal Reserve decision, a surprise in major economic data releases like CPI or payrolls, or a geopolitical escalation that triggers a broad risk-off move. On the upside, a strongly dovish signal from the Fed or a blowout earnings season could push prices above the upper bound. At the one-month horizon, the risks compound further because there are more scheduled events — FOMC meetings, inflation prints, earnings reports — any one of which could generate a multi-standard-deviation move that my intervals would not fully capture.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively normal market functioning. A liquidity event, a flash crash, or a systemic financial stress episode of the kind seen in March 2020 or March 2023 would easily breach even the one-month bounds. These tail events are low probability but not negligible, and they represent the primary reason why realized outcomes over any finite sample will occasionally fall well outside probabilistic forecasts constructed under baseline assumptions.
